scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand it properly.

The person is engaged and planning a small, semi-formal beach wedding. Their mother wants to go wedding dress shopping together at a specific bridal shop that only does white dresses. The person doesn't want a white dress and has already looked up the shop, knowing it only does white. They think the whole white wedding dress thing is stupid, starting with Queen Victoria, so it's not an ancient tradition. They also mention that the ship has sailed on the idea that white symbolizes purity or innocence.

The main reason they're against a white dress is that their mother wore one and got divorced. Every other woman in the family wore colored dresses, and their marriages were long and mostly happy. When the mother asked why they didn't want a white dress, the person first gave the Queen Victoria line, which the mother dismissed. Then they mentioned not being innocent, which was an uncomfortable conversation. The mother pressed further, and eventually, the person admitted that the mother being the only one to break the tradition and get divorced made them not confident in white dresses. The mother got upset, cried, and said that the person spoke to her cruelly, knowing how the divorce affected her. The person hasn't apologized yet and feels the mother backed them into a corner, making them justify their choice when it's their wedding.

So, the question is: Is the person AITA (Are They Acting in a way that's morally Unacceptable)?

First, I need to evaluate the action. The person told their mother that the reason they don't want a white dress is because her divorce made them lose confidence in white dresses. The mother got upset, cried, and felt hurt.

Now, considering the moral aspects. The person is making a choice about their own wedding attire, which is a personal decision. They have the right to choose what they wear. However, the way they communicated their reasons might have been hurtful to their mother.

The person gave several reasons before finally revealing the real reason, which was about the mother's divorce. This could be seen as insensitive because it's bringing up a painful topic. The mother might feel that her past is being used against her, which could be emotionally damaging.

On the other hand, the person felt that their choice shouldn't need justification, especially to their mother. They might feel that their mother was being pushy by repeatedly asking for the real reason. However, the way they handled the situation by revealing the personal reason could be considered unfair or cruel, even if it's true.

So, is it morally acceptable to tell your mother that her past actions (divorce) are the reason you don't want to wear a white dress? It seems like it's crossing a line because it's using the mother's personal history against her, which could cause emotional harm. Even if the person feels justified, the method of communication was hurtful.

Therefore, the action might be morally unacceptable because it caused unnecessary emotional pain to the mother, even if the person's choice is valid.
